Examples include bone, nails, horns, and hooves, which carry out plant-like actions without sensation; or the hands and feet, if sensation is limited to the senses other than touch; or a paralysed hand, which continues to be nourished, since otherwise it would quickly decay. The organ may be called “healthy” in a relative sense. Another possibility is that it cannot be affected by the power—that is, by the directly perceived forms. Since these powers are bodily, their instruments must be affected by their action, at least as a preparation for perception, as the author holds.

“Receptive” may mean receptive alongside the absence of the quality. In that case, “heat” and the other terms mean qualities that can be perceived directly, not merely indirectly, and these bodies can receive them insofar as they can be permeated by the vital spirit. Or “receptive” may mean receptive while the quality is actually present. Then heat and the other terms refer to the qualities in these bodies and instruments, which always have some such qualities. The point is not that matter is itself perceived—matter is not present to a perceiving power. Rather, when the sense power is present and a similar quality reaches it, perception follows, as it does in other comparable cases. These qualities prepare the organ for perception. This is the more likely reading.

The organs can receive a power that exists in them once they are fully prepared for it. They can therefore receive what that power perceives, since a recipient must be suited to what it receives, just as the perceiver must be suited to what it perceives.

“Conditions” and “impediments” are used in their ordinary sense of defining features, as when we say that a human being, on the condition of being able to speak, has this nature, or that a donkey, on the condition of braying, has that nature.

From the perspective of divine metaphysics, all possible existence—the realm of action—is a shadow of the divine realm of unity. That realm in turn follows from the divine attributes, gathered in the simple unity of the divine essence. If the complete order of possible existence, in its downward or upward levels and in its length and breadth, were deficient, existence itself would be deficient. Consider this carefully.

In their terminology, the instruments of perception include the nerves and vital spirit, especially in the language of natural philosophers. That is likely what the author means by “powers in the sensory instruments.” Sometimes “instrument” also means a power considered as an instrument of the soul, as in the definition of the soul as the first perfection of an instrumental body. If “instrument” means a bodily organ, the author’s point is clear. If it means a power, he is denying that the image inheres in the power as a quality, as is commonly supposed. When he says that perception is not the organ’s reaction to an external thing, he is also denying that perception is an effect of the material object itself. The organ’s reaction, together with its position relative to matter bearing a quality, prepares the soul to produce within its own world an image that resembles that quality. On the author’s view, sensation is therefore an active process. The claim he rejects—that perception consists in an image being present in an instrument—is not the same as his claim that the image exists in the perceiver itself. If the instrument means a power, what he rejects is the image’s inherence in that power; what he affirms is that it exists through the power as an expression of the soul.
This supports the earlier point that the recipient must be considered together with the quality actually present in it. The argument here sums up what was just explained.

One might object that this concedes the point: different defining features produce different effects, and sharing a general kind does not help. The author’s point is that the animal’s nutritive power shares something real with the plant’s nutritive power, and also includes sensation and voluntary movement. If the shared “nutritive power” were only a word used in two unrelated ways, or a concept common to two beings that differ completely in their real natures, then the powers of nourishment and sensation would be one and the same. Nourishment would come from the sensitive power, and sensation and movement from the nutritive power, because the general nature would itself differ rather than being specified by distinct features. That is like color, whose general existence is one with the distinctive features that separate its kinds.

But if the shared kind is a real general nature specified in different ways—as with compound bodies, which can be considered as substance, as having dimensions, as body, as growing body, or as sensing body—then the question remains whether the general nature and its distinguishing feature are one existence or several. If sensation and voluntary movement came from the shared, fully formed general nature, plants would also sense and move by choice. Otherwise, the existence of distinct powers is established. This is the philosophers’ view; the author’s own account will be given later, when he defines nourishment and growth and treats powers as simple. The philosophers also hold that effects differing in kind come from different sources. Since the actions of nutritive powers share a kind, they come from a nutritive power of that kind; sensation and voluntary movement differ in kind from nourishment and therefore come from another source. In that sense, their use of “nutritive power” for distinct beings is only verbal: there is no common meaning between powers whose whole natures differ.

The critic assumes that the soul’s existence is confined to the immaterial realm and separate from the lower material world. He finds it unlikely that one thing could be both immaterial and material. He has not understood the soul’s comprehensive unity: through one unified existence, the soul has both an immaterial level and a material level.

The Illuminationists say that God acts through His own self-disclosure: His knowledge of things is identical with their existence. Here, knowledge is not active in the sense of causing an effect; it is identical with the effect itself.

“Form” here means what makes something actual. It may also mean the shared feature of the different meanings of form, or any actual meaning that can be understood. In The Healing, Avicenna uses “form” in several ways: for any intelligible actuality, including separate intellects; for any state or actuality present in a single recipient or in a compound, such as motions and accidents; for what makes matter actual; for what completes matter even without constituting it, as health does; for shapes made in matter by craft; for a thing’s species, broader kind, or distinguishing feature; and for the whole definition, whose general nature may be said to be present in its parts. “Knowledge” here includes both direct awareness and knowledge through a mental representation. In the latter, the image exists in the knower, not in matter. The two kinds of image differ in eight ways, discussed earlier in the section on intellect and intelligible things.
This refers to the other phrase in the passage: the second part of the contrast that answers the first part of the earlier contrast—“what is known is not knowledge.”

The image comes from matter, but has actual existence and perfection; the thing represented is pure potentiality and deficiency. Because the thing is so weak, the image cannot resemble it in the same way an image of a fully actual thing does. In this case, knowledge is stronger than what is known. In the earlier case, what is known is stronger than another knower’s knowledge of it, although it is knowledge of itself.
The knowledge we have of it is still one aspect of it. Consider this carefully.

In truth, the soul, insofar as it produces natural actions, is not aware of itself or of those actions. If knowing the cause entails knowing its effect, then not knowing the cause entails not knowing its effect as well. The soul, in this respect, is nature, since nature is one of its lower levels. Nature is plainly not aware of itself or of its effects.

The author has granted that knowledge of the cause exists, but that knowledge of the effect does not. More precisely, knowledge of the cause does not exist at the soul’s low level in this instance. The soul acts naturally in producing its bodily effects, just as natural powers do. Yet in relation to those powers, which are its own aspects, the soul acts through self-disclosure; its awareness of them is direct and unified. Its knowledge of the powers as they exist at their own levels is like God’s complete, unified knowledge of things through their own existence. The powers here are like the things there: they are relations whose existence depends entirely on the knower.

The First Intellect does not exist at the same level as the lower things of which it is said to be ignorant. If those things’ existence is their knowledge, then the First Intellect’s lack of their existence is its ignorance of them. Yet the First Intellect’s existence is nobler than theirs. Consider this carefully.

This “ignorance” is the absence, in the First Intellect, of a lower level interwoven with nonexistence. The First Intellect contains that level in a higher way, but its own intellectual level is precisely the absence of the lower level. That absence is ignorance; this ignorance is the source of all beings and is nobler than knowledge of those lower things. The philosopher’s words may also mean that the First Intellect is unaware of everything below God because it is absorbed in witnessing divine beauty and majesty. There is a report that God has creatures who do not know that He created Adam or Iblīs. A reading closer to the view held by Aristotle’s followers is this: natural things, considered as material, do not exist as knowledge for the intellect, because they exist in matter, remain hidden by spatial distance and temporal extension, and are not present as unified forms. Knowledge depends on formal existence and presence. They are known through images that exist in the intellect, but in a way that expresses the intellect rather than inhering in it. They may also be said to be known directly in another sense: knowledge is a form present to the knower, and this is true of the thing represented as well as of the image; the image is a tool for attending to the thing, not the thing attended to in itself.

That is, inward insight: the vision of an intellect illuminated by inner awareness, gained through spiritual discipline and exercises that keep the soul turned towards the source of knowledge and its light.
This does not apply to attraction. The body does not seek it by nature; it is harmful to the patient, and the body resists it.

Recall what we said near the beginning of the First Journey about definitions and proofs. The author’s definition of nourishment—and likewise his definition of growth—is a complete demonstration: it gives the full proof. If he had said only “the nutritive power replaces what is lost,” that would be a definition that serves as the starting point of a proof. If he had said only “it changes food so that it resembles the substance being nourished,” that would give the result of the proof.

Maybūdī says that the power should be called “the growth-giving power,” but the philosophers used a name that parallels “nutritive power.” I say that this wording hints at what the author has established: the body is a level of the soul. They describe the power through a bodily feature to point to a kind of unity between body and soul. We can infer the same unity from their calling power “a quality of the soul,” even though it is a quality that exists in the force spread through the muscles. Unless that force were a level of the soul, it would not have a quality of the soul. Hold to this point.

That is, after the age when growth stops, from then until the end of life. The author mentions this case because it makes the difference clearer. Fatness before that age is not growth either; nor is thinness during that age the same as decline.
This refers to the kind of cause called aṭrūqiyā.

In reality, there are two powers here. The wording suggests this by introducing them with “as for,” even though the author has not yet stated that two powers preserve the species. The reproductive power clearly does so. The formative power’s role is less clear, since the body needs the forms of bones, veins, nerves, and flesh, and its individual matter does not need these forms in the same way it needs reproductive moisture to preserve the individual. The answer is that “forms” here means the shapes and patterns that distinguish individuals as members of their kinds. Without the formative power’s work, the kinds would not remain distinct. The test for a cause is whether its absence would entail the absence of its effect. Without reproduction, the species would not continue; without formation and its patterns, the species would not continue as distinct kinds. This does not mean that the individual would immediately cease to exist, since the nutritive power replaces what the body loses. But saying that this individual would no longer remain an individual of its kind amounts to saying that the kind itself would not remain.

Unlike yellow bile and black bile, phlegm has no single organ of its own. It is spread through the other organs because of their moisture and helps keep them from drying out. When the body lacks food, phlegm may be transformed into blood—unless the point is that some of it flows to the brain, and likewise the lungs, to nourish them.

One might say that all this proves only that the fluids are distinguished, not that the nutritive power does the distinguishing; perhaps a separate distinguishing power does that. We reply that attraction already accounts for the distinction: the spleen attracts black bile and the gall bladder attracts yellow bile, for example. A separate power would do no further work and would be an unnecessary, idle addition. Attraction is needed in every organ, while a distinct sorting power is not. Also, the fluids are not entirely separated: a little yellow bile remains in blood to thin it and help it pass through narrow vessels, and a little black bile remains to give it a consistent texture.
This qualification excludes some forms of jaundice caused by a blockage in the bile duct.

The point is that “end” can mean either the point a movement reaches or the purpose for which it is undertaken. Since these are different, they require different powers, just as an animal has an active power and a power of desire. The active power always has an endpoint, even in a pointless or random action: like nature, it brings movement to a particular limit. It carries out its assigned task, but it is not what supplies the purpose. For example, a stone thrown at Zayd’s head reaches and wounds him; the hand’s active power strikes a hated person. But the purpose—relieving the thrower’s anger or making Zayd submit—is the work of desire. These are two different ends and require two sources. The same applies to the plant powers: digestion moves food to the point where its blood form ends, while nourishment acts for the sake of the organ’s form.

Pure matter has no feature that would make it ready for one form rather than another. If the first matter of wheat and barley were exactly the same, there would be no reason for one to become wheat and the other barley. Their elements are the same, but each stage is prepared by the form that came before it: an earlier wheat form prepares matter for the next wheat form, and an earlier barley form prepares it for the next barley form. The same question can be asked about those earlier forms, and so on. The philosophers allow—and indeed require—this succession, so that the flow of existence does not stop. The same applies to a sequence of forms in one matter, as in semen: each new stage, such as a clot or a small lump of flesh, changes what the matter is ready to receive.

The objector would not accept that the inference from “matter alone is not enough” is valid, because he recognizes no agent other than God and considers the matter’s reactions sufficient for the outpouring. The commentator therefore adds the principle that every reaction and readiness in matter depends on an agent’s action.
One argument is specific to the stomach and intestines; the other applies to all the organs.
The difference is that one power may be weak where another is strong, and vice versa. It is not that one of the powers is completely absent.

The food drawn from outside into the stomach is not what nourishes the stomach. The blood drawn from the liver through vessels in the stomach wall nourishes it; the text itself points to this when it mentions what the stomach draws from the liver. The three actions mentioned next concern nourishment of the whole body; the later three concern blood drawn from the liver to nourish the stomach itself. Some copies read “the powers that retain in the substance of the stomach,” which is the better reading.
The commentator means that some writers loosely call this a doubling. More accurately, there are four powers that produce food and four preparatory powers that resemble them.

The four powers that produce nourishment are clear. The four preparatory powers that help digestion and expulsion throughout the body may be understood as follows. Digestion strengthens the qualities of fluids in the stomach. The spleen releases some black bile at the entrance to the stomach, which irritates and contracts it and thereby arouses hunger. The gall bladder releases some yellow bile into the intestine; its irritating quality prompts the bowel to expel its contents. Expulsion also occurs in the testes.
Some copies say “not resembling it.” This may refer to the condition of people with leprosy or vitiligo. Consider the wording carefully.
One might object that plants feed on a simple body, namely water. The answer is that water does not become food for a plant until it mixes with earth.

This is like air around an overturned bowl placed over a fire: when its form is disrupted, the air is prepared to receive the form of water from the giver of forms. In the same way, suitable moist bodies next to the living body prepare its matter to receive the actual form of nourishment from the soul, continuously and through renewed instances. The same idea applies to the body’s light or color: it comes from the soul’s emanations and levels. What the soul preserves is not simply the same material body that remains after death, but a different matter and temperament; the soul is not the immediate cause of the color and shape left behind.

The nature that brings fatigue is also not the same as the nature that serves the soul. The bodily matter, nature, and powers are levels of the soul when considered without restriction, and are linked to it spiritually. Something even more surprising has been said in divine metaphysics: the air that carries speech, or the tablet on which a speaker writes, is not a separate object in the ordinary sense. Considered as the medium of the speaker’s act, the speech exists through the speaker.

The soul is a complete expression of divine unity and bears all the names of God. It has natural qualities as well as the qualities of spiritual beings, potentially or in actuality. So it contains natural powers and bodily aspects in its own right. Just as a higher thing contains the perfections of what is lower in a higher way, the lower effects that flow from it do not make the higher thing lose its level; they are its appearance and expression at lower levels. Some souls possess knowledge and perfection from within themselves, without needing the preparation of hearing or sight. Others acquire them after preparation, but even then the perfection comes from within the soul, not from foreign material things.

The same applies to nourishment. In the senses and intellect, the soul is completed by forms that are present to it directly, not by external things known only indirectly. Its bodily nourishment at the level of nature and body likewise comes from the soul. So the “food from the world of the soul” is not food that is merely potential, even if only nearly ready to nourish: it is food in actuality. And actual food here means its form, not its matter. The author speaks as though food were the matter because, in his view, matter and form are united and matter is absorbed into form. “The world of the soul” means its lower, formal level. This should not seem too strange: the original forms of the organs come from the soul, since the formative power is a lower level of the soul; the replacement of what those organs lose comes from the soul as well. The soul brings together the worlds of meaning and form. It is like clear air touched by a cold wind: clouds appear without vapour rising from below, yet the air does not leave its own higher state.
Forgive this long explanation. This is a difficult point and a common source of doubt and missteps.

At every moment, the body that is nourished is made up of different parts from the body at the previous moment. The whole would cease to exist whenever any part disappeared. That is not so if the stages of its form appear through one enduring, individual soul, which remains the source of all the stages. This applies the principle already mentioned: every natural or psychic substance is one thing in actuality. Keep this point in mind.

The perceiver must be one with what it perceives; otherwise it would not be completed by it or move from potentiality to actuality. This is the major premise of an unstated argument: the sense is completed by what it senses, and whatever is completed by something is identical with it. Therefore the sense is identical with what it senses.

Just as the intellect has four stages, from intellect in potentiality to intellect in actuality, digestion also has four stages, from food in potentiality to food in actuality. The note may instead compare the four degrees of abstraction in knowledge: perception by the senses abstracts from matter while requiring the presence of matter; imagination does not require matter, though its images retain shape, size, and similar features; estimation is more abstract, though its objects remain tied to measurable things; and intellect is fully abstract and free of matter. The four stages of cleansing and digesting food follow the same pattern. The author’s phrase “understanding” in place of “knowledge” is not a serious problem, since all forms are present to the intellect, as he has explained and will explain again. The separate discussion of digestion stages in this chapter may not fully match the chapter heading, but that is a minor point.
An abscess is a large, hot swelling; a boil is a broader term and can include cold swellings.

This wording suggests that the end of this digestion comes when food reaches the stomach, where another digestion also takes place. The usual view is that there is only one digestion in the stomach. One could say that the first digestion is completed there, though it begins in the mouth: “completed” would mean perfected or brought to its fullest stage. The four stages are the four main visible transformations in a fully developed animal. In fact, food changes at every moment from the time it is chewed until it becomes part of an organ, so its transformations cannot be limited to four.
The word “of” may explain which powers these are, or where they come from: they may be the governing nature itself, in its branches and stages, or powers that arise from nature.

The account is not quite right. The mesenteric vessels carry the finer part of food, after it has been fully digested in the stomach, toward the vessels leading to the liver. It seems the phrase about reaching the liver originally followed the words “to another level, the liver,” and was moved here by a copyist. The author would not have mistaken the role of the mesentery.

This is the third place where the two powers are defined. The first definition comes from Avicenna; the second appears incidentally at the end of the division of powers; this third one is the main definition here. The phrase “in their true sense” signals that the earlier definition was only nominal, since it came before the existence of these powers was established. As Avicenna says in The Healing, definitions given before a thing's existence is proved are nominal definitions; once it is proved, the same definitions become real ones.

Nourishment occurs directly, while growth occurs through nourishment. Since the nutritive power acts through three operations, some say it is only a conceptual unity: the power that gathers food, joins it to the body, and changes it into the body's substance. The fuller account is that it is one power with different aspects and stages, just as the chief of all the powers—the soul's commanding light—is one, and the other powers are its modes and expressions. As the Persian saying puts it, “In the house, all is the householder.”
The phrase “natural ends” excludes ends chosen by will, since a change in chosen ends does not by itself mean a change in the one who chooses.

Another proof, besides the difference in ends, is that the actions themselves differ and the two powers can operate independently. The nutritive power brings about a qualitative change, using digestion and then adhesion; it also produces the body's substantial forms. The growth power brings about a weak, gradual change in quantity.

Fire changes air. An opponent could therefore say that the nutritive power is air, since both it and air “nourish”: air is said to nourish fire by changing into it. But air destroys fire by changing it into itself; otherwise the fire would rise to the sphere of ether or become earth.

The point is that bodily powers, insofar as they are bodily, cannot act without limit. But insofar as they are connected to intelligible and immaterial things, they may do so: through that connection they serve as powers and instruments of those things. Still, since they are also connected to matter and body, the continued flow of intelligible forms into them depends on the recipient's continuing to exist. A recipient made of parts with opposing natures, each tending to separate from the others, cannot last forever. Otherwise those parts would be prevented from acting according to their own natures and forced to do the opposite, which is impossible according to the philosophers.
Since the appeal to the body being made up of basic elements is the same as the second argument, the author says he will examine that argument.

The discussion concerns the loss of the moisture supplied by food; what weakens the nutritive power is the loss of the body's innate moisture, which sustains its natural heat. There is no circle. The innate moisture declines through the weakening of the cause that sustains it. A thing disappears or weakens when the cause that keeps it present or strong is absent; it may also weaken because of some other cause, such as increased heat. Two things that depend on one another—especially when one exists in the other—may decline together, each in a different causal respect. For example, when matter loses its form, that form's individual existence ends; when the form disappears, the matter also ceases to exist. Here, the form preserves the body's material organization. As the form weakens, the material becomes less stable; that, in turn, weakens the form's activity further, though in a new degree. The process continues until the body breaks down.

The objection is that a longer period of nourishment does not help, since a natural power acts steadily and accidental causes do not simply join it. The answer is that the forces consuming moisture grow stronger because of poor care of food, air, and other necessary conditions. Even a careful, wise, medically trained person, who watches over their health and does everything they can, cannot know all the events decreed for them or ward off every stroke of chance. One may object that poor care also occurs in youth, and that nourishment repairs the damage. The reply is that such chance events weaken not only the body's mixture and the matter that receives it, but also the power and agent. The nutritive power cannot make good all the damage; it too keeps weakening. It is like someone pitching a tent in a storm that blows from every direction. Each time the wind twists the tent and threatens to bring it down, the person repairs it, raising the poles and tightening the pegs. But as the wind shakes the tent's supports, it also weakens the person doing the repairs, until the person is exhausted and the tent collapses.

Since things are naturally inclined to seek their own good and perfection, nothing acts by its nature in a way that leads to its own destruction. The natural heat's gradual drying of moisture must therefore be a form of completion. Once it has reached completion, it no longer needs that connection, so its relation to the moisture ends. Understand this if you are able, and do not be heedless.

The author is considering the issue from the standpoint of divine causes; this note addresses natural causes, though it too is sound. As for the claim that semen's temperament is finer and stronger, the key is to distinguish mature, firmly established moisture from a finer temperament. Moisture, understood as a substance that binds the original organs together—especially the heart—is not the same as temperament, which is an attribute. Even if this moisture comes from semen, the argument concerns the moisture in the organs, one of the four secondary humours described by physicians. It is clearly original and innate, unlike later or foreign moisture. To deny this is unreasonable. The objection that a more balanced temperament should at once give rise to the soul's powers is also answered by the fact that the temperament of a young adult is more balanced than that of an older person, even though the latter has fuller mental powers, especially inward speech and thought. These powers do not flow into semen at the outset: it does not yet contain the heart, brain, and liver, where the three vital spirits reside. Rather, the powers and perfections flow through those spirits. Yet without semen and the original, governing organs, no such perfections would arise at all.

This objection is extremely weak. Seminal moisture—the secondary moisture that binds the organs—does not disappear until death, even in a body that has become thin and fragile. Could one say that naturally moist skin, even after being soaked in water, contains no moisture of its own?

Who restricted it to those particular vessels? The issue is whether original moisture is stronger and firmer than moisture acquired later, not whether one temperament is stronger than another. What does this objection have to do with that?

This is a subtle allusion. The main point is that mixing foreign moisture with moisture from food weakens its quality and makes it less like the body's own moisture. It is called a subtle allusion because the third argument says that even the best chyle cannot replace what the original organs lose: its quality is too different, not merely because it has mixed with foreign moisture.

The author does not mention the “originated” being, though he is setting out to list all the rational possibilities. Here, “originated” has a broad sense: a generated thing is preceded by both matter and time, while an originated thing is not; it is the opposite of this combined condition. “Complete” and “incomplete” are not used in their usual sense of having, or lacking, a further state to reach. The author himself says that some incomplete beings are self-sufficient souls, not things made to become matter for something else. Nor are the souls of the heavenly spheres merely supposed to last forever; they are held to do so in fact. Here “complete” means a being that is not made to serve as matter or a means for another being; “incomplete” means one that does serve this role. Elsewhere, the author says that every being is either complete or incomplete, and that complete beings may be above perfection or simply perfect, while incomplete beings may or may not be self-sufficient.

One might ask why a body's complete cause could not preserve its life through an endless succession of motions, just as successive motions preserve it for a time during its life. This proof and the following point about complete beings appear to form one argument: it proceeds from substantial motion to the claim that each level of a moving being has an end. Plants, animals, and human beings are levels along this motion, and the moving being must pass from one level to the next; natural death is that transition. The proof is sound, though the claim that a plant's end is to feed an animal, and an animal's end is to feed a human, needs qualification. It concerns a plant on the way to animal life, serving as its matter, and an animal on the way to human life—not a fully formed plant such as an almond tree or a complete animal such as a horse or cow. It would be strange to call a tree's becoming food for an animal its natural death, rather than an accidental death, and the same is true of animals. Keep this distinction in mind.
The purpose belongs naturally to the rational soul, though not to the estimative faculty.

This points back to the earlier argument that composite bodies cannot be sustained indefinitely, even if the nutritive power continually replaced what was lost. If the soul were always turned toward this world and used its powers, it would keep providing the replacement. But by nature it is always turning toward its goal and independence from the body. Likewise, if bodily powers could act without limit, the rational soul would set them aside once it reached its goal. Since the soul naturally turns toward God and is little concerned with the body, the body breaks down.
The soul's manifestation of dominion is a perfection in its existence, even if it is a moral failing. Whether through mercy or power, the soul no longer needs the body's natural functions.
That is, human souls bearing the traits of non-speaking animals do not have a spiritual fire; they are consumed by the fire of nature.

The person meant may be al-Ghazali; the disagreement may be only about words. By “angels” the philosophers may mean those who govern events, not the highest ranks of angels who stand before God and are too exalted to manage bodily matter. This applies if “powers” means causes that are separate from bodies or joined to them, rather than beings tied to time and matter. Those temporal beings work within matter and are the places where its changes take place.

That is, the Muʿtazilites say one action produces another. The truth is that everything happens through God's power; nothing else acts independently. But the Muʿtazilites say that an effect does not need God in order to continue existing. If God were absent, they claim, it would make no difference to the thing's own being. In their view, God makes things independent in themselves and in their actions. Philosophers instead treat other causes as means through which God's generosity flows, not as independent creators. The Ashʿarites reject these means and deny all cause and effect between created things.

For us, there is no difficulty in explaining how an unaware formative power can produce well-ordered results. Order alone does not prove awareness; we see ordered actions in nature. We have also shown that powers have direct awareness of themselves and their actions.

This does not mean that semen is already an animal; it is matter that still needs a form. The problem is that the argument says it contains some part from every organ, which would make it a complete body with organs. The reference to the “problem returning” points to the claim that the animal should be a sphere. If the parts of semen differ, that difference leads to an impossible circle or endless chain. Once that difference is rejected, the original problem returns. There is no contradiction between the two objections: the first assumes the parts are alike, while the second follows from the claim that they differ.

At first this may look like the familiar problem of which came first, the egg or the chicken. One might also ask why the cause must differ; why could the matter's readiness not be enough? Philosophers often explain differences between individuals by different matter, and the differences in matter by earlier forms, in a sequence that continues over time. But here the organs differ by kind. Different readiness in matter cannot explain differences between kinds; the active cause, or its different aspects, must also differ. The causes must exist together, so the chain would be simultaneous, not a sequence through time.
Since the question concerns the cause of the difference itself, the endless chain would have to exist all at once. It would not be a series of causes following one another over time.
The circle and endless chain are impossible here because the things that depend on one another are active causes arranged in order, not passive materials that receive forms.

Since animal organs differ by kind, differences in the matter that receives them are not enough to explain them. The active cause or its aspects must differ too. This resembles the view of some Persian philosophers that distinct kinds in this lower world are shadows of distinct higher beings, and the view of other philosophers that different aspects of the Active Intellect give rise to different kinds.

The pleasure meant is bodily pleasure. The commentary explains it by saying that semen contains many spirits and much heat, which stimulate and rub against the place from which it is released. Once it leaves, the body feels relief and ease, and the friction and pain end.
The words “those parts” are missing from some copies. The editor considers the shorter reading, without them, more likely to be correct.

A child may resemble a parent in the roots of the nails or hair, even if no part of the nail itself is carried in semen. An illness at a nail root may affect the nail, and heat at a hair root may darken the hair. Resemblance is direct at the roots and indirect in the nails or hair themselves.

The objection is that bodily arrangement as a whole may resemble between parent and child even when particular parts do not. For example, a parent's nose may be hooked and the child's flat, though both noses are placed in relation to the mouth in a similar way. If semen comes from the whole body, the general arrangement may resemble even when a particular feature does not; some obstacle may prevent that particular resemblance.
This can be denied, as the author has said earlier. The argument may mean only that semen would contain different organs, as a dead embryo does, not that it is already a living animal.
This can also be denied. Perhaps the woman's emission helps the man's semen form the child but does not itself produce another child. This also answers the next argument.

The commentator suggests that a child's sex depends on which semen is stronger: the man's or the woman's. If the man's semen overpowers the woman's and changes it to its own temperament, the child's body takes on male traits.
The example is the mule. Some copies say “not of its kind,” meaning not of the same species.
This means the author's proof goes further than Aristotle's position. Matter, in every case, is indeterminate and only potentially what it may become; it is not yet a complete, actual thing.

Semen is not fully formed even as a distinct kind of matter, much less as a complete body with nerves, ligaments, bones, and other parts. This is related to the verse: “The human being was created weak.” The argument assumes that semen's different parts would themselves produce the organs, without needing a formative or reproductive power. If the argument only means that different parts of matter help the powers form organs, this objection does not apply.

Being closer to readiness for a particular organ does not mean that semen already differs in kind. A thing can be closer to becoming something and still not be that thing. Unless every way it could fail to become that thing is closed off, it is not yet actual.

The commentator replies that even if al-Razi accepts that food only prepares matter to receive forms from within, this still supports the objection. Different organs are fed by different powers, and their food may therefore differ after the fourth digestion. Can the soul create distinct forms of sensation directly, without prior sensory material to prepare it?
The waste need only resemble what it replaces; it need not be identical or equally strong. The bran of flour resembles the grain, and the sediment of a liquid resembles the liquid closely enough.

The question about preserving the order of the parts is valid if the claim is that they keep their positions after being separated from the organs. But if the claim is only that the parts differ in kind, then separating them and bringing them together does not make their differences disappear.

The source of weakness need not be only psychic; natural causes also have an effect, and this cannot be doubted. The claim that a flowing fluid cannot contain differences in arrangement is also challenged in another copy: mixtures such as milk and vinegar contain different powers. This is a separate objection to the author's point.

Because the organs are made from the material of semen, the author gives this brief reminder of the main argument for why bodily matter cannot explain their different forms. He has already set out the core of it.

One might ask why the Throne has four supports, as the reports say. First, Azazil acts only in this world, unlike the four angels, whose actions appear in the inner worlds and extend toward the divine presence. Second, evil exists only as a consequence, not as something created for its own sake. The partial appearances of these angels sometimes seen by prophets and saints may be stronger and clearer than their universal source. In light, intellect, and mercy, the source is stronger than its appearance; in darkness, ignorance, and anger, the appearance can seem stronger than its source.
The cited philosopher's point is that the formative power is one level of the soul.

The soul has a unified whole. Its “organs” are the body's subtle spirits and parts; its “qualities” are luminous features that exist within the soul's unity. Its powers are aspects of that unity, like shadows of those qualities.

Just as the things matter may receive differ in actuality, its potential readiness for them also differs. One cannot say that the remote readiness is actual while the different readinesses are only potential; the discussion applies to all degrees of readiness.
What makes matter ready is its temperament, unless one follows the view, discussed in the First Journey, that “readiness” and temperament name the same quality.
